sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 4: Service Level Objectives
findings: An SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the service level; an SLO is a target value or range for an SLI; an SLA is an agreement with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing the SLOs it contains (no explicit consequence means it is an SLO).
Most metrics are better thought of as distributions than averages; an average latency hides a long tail of much slower requests.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 3: Embracing Risk
findings: The error budget is the difference between the SLO and measured reliability over a window; while budget remains, new releases can be pushed.
Example: an SLO of 99.999 percent of queries gives an error budget of 0.001 percent; a problem failing 0.0002 percent spends 20 percent of the quarter's budget.

sources.title: The Site Reliability Workbook, Appendix B: Example Error Budget Policy
findings: If the service has exceeded its error budget for the preceding four-week window, halt all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes until it is back within its SLO.
The policy is not a punishment; it gives the team permission to focus on reliability when data says reliability matters more than features.
sources.limits: An example policy; thresholds are illustrative.

sources.title: The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 5: Alerting on SLOs
findings: Alert on the rate at which the error budget is being spent (burn rate); multiple burn rates and windows page fast for high error rates and file a ticket for low but sustained ones.
Multiwindow burn-rate alerts give good precision and recall at the cost of more thresholds to manage.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems
findings: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation; track the latency of failed requests too, since a slow error is worse than a fast one.
Monitoring answers what is broken (the symptom) and why (the cause); the distinction keeps signal high and noise low.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 22: Addressing Cascading Failures
findings: Always use randomized exponential backoff for retries, limit retries per request, consider a server-wide retry budget, and avoid retrying at several layers, which multiplies attempts.

Load shedding drops some traffic near overload (for example HTTP 503 above a number of in-flight requests); keep queues short relative to the thread pool so overload is rejected early; propagate deadlines and cancellations down the call stack.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 5: Eliminating Toil
findings: Toil is work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as the service grows.
Overhead (meetings, HR) and grungy work with lasting value are not toil.

sources.title: The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 10: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
findings: Leaders model and enforce blameless behavior and blameless language in postmortems; blameful questions put people on the defensive and stifle collaboration.
A postmortem looks for the system change (training, tooling, process) that prevents recurrence rather than a person to blame.

sources.title: Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres (Brandur Leach)
findings: An idempotency key is a unique client-generated value sent with a request; the server records the request's state under it, resumes on retry with the same key, and returns the stored result once the request finished.
Split a request into atomic phases (local mutations in one transaction) between foreign state mutations, and store a recovery point after each so a retry resumes where it failed.
A non-idempotent foreign state mutation that fails indeterminately (timeout, connection reset) cannot be retried safely and is marked failed.
sources.limits: Postgres and Ruby examples; publication date read from the article.

sources.title: Transactionally Staged Job Drains in Postgres (Brandur Leach)
findings: Stage jobs in a table inside the same database transaction as the data change, so they stay invisible until commit; a separate enqueuer moves them to the job queue and deletes the rows.
This avoids jobs that run before their data is committed or that are lost when the transaction rolls back.
sources.limits: Postgres and Sidekiq examples; publication date read from the article.

sources.title: Logs vs Structured Events (Charity Majors)
findings: Replace log lines and log levels with arbitrarily wide structured events that describe the request and its context, one event per request per service.
Disconnected metrics and loglevel:ERROR lines cannot give explorable, ad hoc data.
sources.limits: Opinionated practitioner post by an observability vendor's cofounder.

sources.title: Observability: A Manifesto (Charity Majors, Honeycomb)
findings: Observability is the power to ask new questions of a system without shipping new code or gathering new data; monitoring covers known unknowns, observability unknown unknowns.
It needs raw events rather than pre-aggregation, high-cardinality fields (user, request id, cart id) as group-by dimensions, and structured data.
sources.limits: Vendor blog; the page shows no reliable original publication date.

sources.title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP (Martin Kleppmann)
findings: Linearizability (consistency in the CAP sense): if operation B starts after operation A completed, B sees the state as of A's completion or newer.

Stop labeling systems CP or AP and use more precise terminology for the trade-offs (linearizability, causal consistency, read your writes, monotonic reads). The diagrams preview Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
sources.limits: 2015 blog post by the author of Designing Data-Intensive Applications.

sources.title: Hermitage: Testing transaction isolation levels (Martin Kleppmann)
findings: Test cases show which anomalies each database's isolation levels prevent, including lost update (P4), read skew (G-single), and write skew (G2-item, G2); default levels often allow them.
The SQL standard's isolation level definitions are flawed and databases implement the same names differently, so the anomaly, not the level name, is what to check.
sources.limits: Results per database version at test time; repository maintained irregularly.

sources.title: How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)
findings: A lock holder can pause (GC, network) past its lease and write after another client took the lock; include a fencing token, a number that increases on every acquisition, and have storage reject writes with an older token.
A lock used for correctness, not just efficiency, needs fencing; storage must check the token.
sources.limits: Blog post; part of the Redlock debate.

sources.title: The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 2: Implementing SLOs
findings: A system with monitoring but no formal objectives, no error budget, and an unspoken goal of 100 percent uptime is the starting state to move away from.
An error budget approach needs stakeholder-approved SLOs, agreement that they are achievable, a written error budget policy, and a process to refine the SLO.
